sections.title: Detailed Brief Overview
rows: Topic Definition (परिभाषा)
**Parts of Speech (शब्द भेद)** are categories into which words are classified according to their syntactic and grammatical functions within a sentence.
Scope in UPSSSC PET
Direct testing in **General English (सामान्य अंग्रेजी)** section: Spotting Errors, Sentence Improvement, Fill in the Blanks, and Reading Comprehension context questions.
Core Functional Categories

Contains **8 essential classes**: Noun (संज्ञा), Pronoun (सर्वनाम), Verb (क्रिया), Adjective (विशेषण), Adverb (क्रियाविशेषण), Preposition (संबंधसूचक अव्यय), Conjunction (समुच्चयबोधक अव्यय), and Interjection (विस्मयादिबोधक).
Fundamental Subject-Verb Formula
**Singular Subject → Singular Verb** | **Plural Subject → Plural Verb**. Rule applies strictly across all tenses and structures.
Modifier Core Rules
**Adjectives** modify only Nouns/Pronouns. **Adverbs** modify Verbs, Adjectives, or other Adverbs.
Connector Core Rules
**Prepositions** show spatial/temporal relationships between nouns. **Conjunctions** join words, phrases, or clauses.
Exam Weightage & Importance
Forms **100% of the foundational base** for UPSSSC PET English questions (Grammar + Comprehension).
Primary Error Categories Tested
Subject-Verb Agreement, Incorrect Preposition Usage, Misplaced Modifiers, Uncountable Noun Pluralization, and Correlative Conjunction Pairing.

items.title: Rule 1: Noun (संज्ञा) & Uncountable Noun Rules with Mnemonic **SING-UN**
items.content:
• **Uncountable Nouns** (e.g., *Advice, Furniture, Information, Scenery, Luggage, Equipment, Hair, Work*) NEVER take 'a/an' or plural 's/es'.
• They ALWAYS take a **singular verb**.
• To express quantity, use phrases like **'a piece of'**, **'an item of'**, or **'articles of'**.
• **Mnemonic SING-UN:** **S**cenery, **I**nformation, **N**ews, **G**old = **U**ncountable & **N**ever plural.
• **Example 1:** Incorrect: *The sceneries of Kashmir are breathtaking.* | **Correct:** **The scenery of Kashmir is breathtaking.**
• **Example 2:** Incorrect: *He gave me many advices.* | **Correct:** **He gave me many pieces of advice.**
• **Example 3:** Incorrect: *All the furnitures were sold.* | **Correct:** **All the furniture was sold.**
• **Example 4:** Incorrect: *I have an urgent work today.* | **Correct:** **I have a piece of urgent work today.**
• **Example 5:** Incorrect: *Her hairs are black.* | **Correct:** **Her hair is black.**

items.title: Rule 2: Pronoun (सर्वनाम) Agreement & Relative Cases with Mnemonic **WHO-SUB / WHOM-OBJ**
items.content:
• **Subject Case vs Object Case:** Use nominative pronouns (*I, he, she, they, who*) as subjects and objective pronouns (*me, him, her, them, whom*) as objects.
• Use **'Who'** for Subject position (does the action) and **'Whom'** for Object position (receives the action).
• When pronouns are connected by **'and/or'**, test each pronoun separately by dropping the other.
• **Mnemonic WHO-SUB / WHOM-OBJ:** **Who** = Subject (replaces *He/She*); **Whom** = Object (replaces *Him/Her*).
• **Example 1:** Incorrect: *Him and I went to Lucknow.* | **Correct:** **He and I went to Lucknow.**
• **Example 2:** Incorrect: *Between you and I, this plan is secret.* | **Correct:** **Between you and me, this plan is secret.** (Prepositions take objective case).
• **Example 3:** Incorrect: *The boy whom scored top marks was awarded.* | **Correct:** **The boy who scored top marks was awarded.**
• **Example 4:** Incorrect: *Who did you invite to the party?* | **Correct:** **Whom did you invite to the party?**
• **Example 5:** Incorrect: *It was me who called you.* | **Correct:** **It was I who called you.** (Complement of verb 'to be' takes nominative case).

items.title: Rule 3: Subject-Verb Agreement (SVA) with Mnemonic **NEAR-NOR & ALONG-FIRST**
items.content:
• When subjects are joined by **'Neither...nor'**, **'Either...or'**, or **'Not only...but also'**, the verb agrees with the **NEAREST subject**.
• When subjects are joined by **'along with'**, **'together with'**, **'as well as'**, **'with'**, or **'besides'**, the verb agrees strictly with the **FIRST subject**.
• **Mnemonic NEAR-NOR:** *Nor/Or* = Verb targets the **Nearest** noun.
• **Mnemonic ALONG-FIRST:** *Along/As well as* = Verb targets the **First** noun.
• **Example 1:** Incorrect: *Neither the teacher nor the students was present.* | **Correct:** **Neither the teacher nor the students were present.**
• **Example 2:** Incorrect: *Neither the students nor the teacher were present.* | **Correct:** **Neither the students nor the teacher was present.**
• **Example 3:** Incorrect: *The PM along with his ministers are visiting UP.* | **Correct:** **The PM along with his ministers is visiting UP.**
• **Example 4:** Incorrect: *Ramesh as well as his friends have passed.* | **Correct:** **Ramesh as well as his friends has passed.**
• **Example 5:** Incorrect: *Either you or he are wrong.* | **Correct:** **Either you or he is wrong.**

items.title: Rule 4: Adjectives (विशेषण) & Latin Comparatives Rule with Mnemonic **LATIN-TO**
items.content:
• Adjectives ending in **'-ior'** (*Senior, Junior, Superior, Inferior, Prior, Anterior, Posterior*) and the word **'Preferable'** are followed by **'to'**, NEVER **'than'**.
• Do NOT use double comparatives (*more wiser*) or double superlatives (*most highest*).
• Order of Adjectives mnemonic: **OSASCOMP** (Opinion, Size, Age, Shape, Color, Origin, Material, Purpose).
• **Mnemonic LATIN-TO:** Words ending in **-IOR** MUST link with **TO**, not *THAN*.
• **Example 1:** Incorrect: *He is senior than me in service.* | **Correct:** **He is senior to me in service.**
• **Example 2:** Incorrect: *Milk is more preferable than tea.* | **Correct:** **Milk is preferable to tea.**
• **Example 3:** Incorrect: *She is more wiser than her sister.* | **Correct:** **She is wiser than her sister.**
• **Example 4:** Incorrect: *This is the most cleanest city.* | **Correct:** **This is the cleanest city.**
• **Example 5:** Incorrect: *This task is prior than that one.* | **Correct:** **This task is prior to that one.**

items.title: Rule 5: Prepositions (संबंधसूचक अव्यy) & Confusing Pairs with Mnemonic **B2-A3+**
items.content:
• **Between** is used for **2 people/things**. **Among** is used for **more than 2**.
• **Beside** means *'by the side of'* (पास में). **Besides** means *'in addition to'* (के अलावा).
• Direct transitive verbs (*discuss, describe, reach, order, attack, resemblance, marry*) do NOT take prepositions after them in active voice.
• **Mnemonic B2-A3+:** **B**etween = **2** entities | **A**mong = **3+** entities.
• **Example 1:** Incorrect: *Distribute the sweets between the five children.* | **Correct:** **Distribute the sweets among the five children.**
• **Example 2:** Incorrect: *He sat besides me during the class.* | **Correct:** **He sat beside me during the class.**
• **Example 3:** Incorrect: *We discussed about the PET exam syllabus.* | **Correct:** **We discussed the PET exam syllabus.**
• **Example 4:** Incorrect: *She reached at the railway station late.* | **Correct:** **She reached the railway station late.**
• **Example 5:** Incorrect: *Besides English, he speaks French.* | **Correct:** **Besides English, he speaks French.** (Correct usage: In addition to).

items.title: Rule 6: Correlative Conjunctions & Inversion with Mnemonic **NO-THAN / HARD-WHEN**
items.content:
• Fixed Pair 1: **No sooner...than** (NEVER pair with *when* or *then*).
• Fixed Pair 2: **Hardly / Scarcely...when** (NEVER pair with *than* or *then*).
• When a sentence starts with negative adverbs (*No sooner, Hardly, Scarcely, Barely*), apply **Subject-Verb Inversion** (Auxiliary Verb comes BEFORE Subject).
• **Mnemonic NO-THAN & HARD-WHEN:** **No sooner → THAN** | **Hardly → WHEN**.
• **Example 1:** Incorrect: *No sooner had I reached the station when the train left.* | **Correct:** **No sooner had I reached the station than the train left.**
• **Example 2:** Incorrect: *Hardly had she entered the room than the phone rang.* | **Correct:** **Hardly had she entered the room when the phone rang.**
• **Example 3:** Incorrect: *No sooner he saw the police than he ran away.* | **Correct:** **No sooner did he see the police than he ran away.** (Inversion enforced).
• **Example 4:** Incorrect: *Scarcely had we started then it began to rain.* | **Correct:** **Scarcely had we started when it began to rain.**
• **Example 5:** Incorrect: *He not only lost his ticket but also his luggage.* | **Correct:** **He lost not only his ticket but also his luggage.** (Parallel structure).

sections.title: Comprehensive Rule & Classification Tables
rows: Uncountable Nouns (अगणनीय संज्ञा)
Cannot take plural suffix (-s/-es) or articles 'a/an'. Takes singular verb always.

• Advice, Furniture, Information, Luggage, Equipment, Scenery, Poetry, Knowledge.
• **Example:** *His knowledge of English is vast.*
Plural in Form, Singular in Meaning
Words ending in '-s' that represent a single subject/disease/game. Takes singular verb.

• Physics, Mathematics, News, Innings, Economics, Rickets, Billiards, Darts.
• **Example:** *Mathematics is an interesting subject.*
Plural Nouns without '-s'
Nouns representing a collective body in plural. Takes plural verb strictly.

• People, Cattle, Poultry, Gentry, Peasantry, Clergy, Children, Folk.
• **Example:** *Cattle are grazing in the field.*
Distributive Pronouns (Each / Every / Either / Neither)
Followed by 'of the' + Plural Noun + **Singular Verb** + Singular Possessive (his/her).

• Each of / Either of / Neither of + Plural Noun + Singular Verb.
• **Example:** *Each of the boys has submitted his assignment.*
Relative Pronoun Cases (Who vs Whom)

Who = Nominative case (Subject role).
Whom = Objective case (Object role).

• *Who wrote this book?* (Subject)
• *To whom were you speaking?* (Object)
Stative Verbs (No Continuous Tense)
Verbs of perception/emotion cannot be used in Progressive (-ing) tense for states.

• See, Hear, Smell, Taste, Know, Understand, Love, Hate, Remember, Belong.
• **Incorrect:** *I am knowing him.* → **Correct:** *I know him.*
Adjective Order Formula (OSASCOMP)
Order when multiple adjectives describe a noun.

• **O**pinion, **S**ize, **A**ge, **S**hape, **C**olor, **O**rigin, **M**aterial, **P**urpose.
• **Example:** *A beautiful small old round red Indian wooden table.*
Adverbs of Frequency Placement
Placed BEFORE main verb, but AFTER helping verb (be, is, am, are, was, were).

• Always, Never, Seldom, Often, Usually, Hardly, Rarely.
• **Example:** *He always comes late.* | *She is always happy.*
Fixed Prepositions: Verb + Preposition
Specific verbs require fixed prepositions regardless of Hindi translations.

• Accused **of**, Abide **by**, Prevail **upon**, Refrain **from**, Congratulate **on**, Abstain **from**, Adapt **to**.
• **Example:** *He was accused of theft.*
Fixed Prepositions: Adjective + Preposition
Specific adjectives take exact prepositions.

• Interested **in**, Good **at**, Senior **to**, Jealous **of**, Similar **to**, Aware **of**, Fond **of**.
• **Example:** *She is good at English.*
Correlative Conjunction Pairs
Conjunctions that must always occur in pairs with parallel structure.

• Either...or, Neither...nor, Both...and, Not only...but also, Whether...or, Though...yet.
• **Example:** *Though he worked hard, yet he failed.*

items.term: Trick 1: The 'OSASCOMP' Rule for Adjective Order
items.definition: Memorize the sequence: **O**pinion (**O**nly), **S**ize (**S**mart), **A**ge (**A**nd), **S**hape (**S**harp), **C**olor (**C**ats), **O**rigin (**O**vercome), **M**aterial (**M**any), **P**urpose (**P**roblems). Always arrange multiple adjectives in this sequence.
Coordinating conjunctions linking independent clauses are remembered by **FANBOYS**: **F**or, **A**nd, **N**or, **B**ut, **O**r, **Y**et, **S**o. Example: **He was tired, yet he kept working.**
Associate **No Sooner** with comparative ending **-er**, which ALWAYS matches **THAN**. Associate **Hardly/Scarcely** with **WHEN**. **No Sooner = THAN | Hardly = WHEN**.

Any comparative adjective ending in **-IOR** (*Superior, Inferior, Senior, Junior, Prior*) along with **Preferable** strictly takes **TO**, never *than*. Example: **This coffee is superior to that one.**

Identify Nouns instantly by checking word endings: **-tion** (*Action*), **-ment** (*Management*), **-ness** (*Kindness*), **-ity** (*Ability*), **-ance/-ence** (*Importance/Patience*), **-ship** (*Friendship*).
Most adverbs of manner are formed by adding **-ly** to adjectives (*Quick → Quickly, Beautiful → Beautifully*). Exception: *Fast, Hard, Late* act as both Adjective and Adverb without changing form.

items.term: Trick 7: The Transitive Verb Preposition Elimination Trick
items.definition: Do NOT add prepositions after active voice verbs like: **Discuss, Describe, Reach, Order, Attack, Resemble, Enter**. Say **'Discuss the topic'**, NOT *'Discuss about the topic'*.
Candidates write *informations*, *furnitures*, or *sceneries*. Uncountable nouns NEVER take '-s/-es'. Always write: **pieces of information**, **items of furniture**, **scenery**.
Writing *'Senior than me'* or *'Preferable than tea'*. Latin comparative adjectives ending in **-ior** and the word **preferable** MUST take **'to'**.
Pairing *No sooner...when* or *Hardly...than*. **No sooner** MUST pair with **than**. **Hardly/Scarcely** MUST pair with **when**.

items.term: Mistake 4: Subject-Verb Mismatch in 'Along with' / 'As well as'
items.definition: Making the verb agree with the noun nearest to it instead of the real subject. In *'The Captain along with his sailors was saved'*, verb agrees with **Captain** (singular).

items.term: Mistake 5: Using Double Comparatives or Superlatives
items.definition: Using *more wiser*, *more better*, or *most highest*. Use only one comparative/superlative modifier: **wiser**, **better**, **highest**.
**Beside** means *'by the side of'* (at the side). **Besides** means *'in addition to'*. Example: **Sit beside me** vs **Besides English, I know Hindi**.
Placing adverbs like *always, never, seldom* in the wrong position. Place them **BEFORE main verbs** (*He always works*) and **AFTER auxiliary verbs** (*He is always punctual*).
Nouns name persons, places, things, or concepts. Uncountable nouns take singular verbs and no direct articles ('a/an').
Pronouns replace nouns. Case consistency is vital: Subjective (*I, he, she, who*) vs Objective (*me, him, her, whom*).
*Each of / Every one of / Either of / Neither of* takes a **Plural Noun** followed by a **Singular Verb** and **Singular Possessive Pronoun**.
Verbs express action or state. Verbs must strictly agree with the subject in number and person.
With *Either...or* and *Neither...nor*, the verb agrees with the **nearest subject**.
With *as well as, along with, together with, with, besides*, the verb agrees with the **first subject**.
Adjectives modify nouns/pronouns. Follow **OSASCOMP** for ordering multiple adjectives.
Adjectives ending in *-ior* (*Senior, Junior, Superior, Inferior*) and *Preferable* take **'to'**, never 'than'.
Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Adverbs of frequency go before main verbs.
Prepositions show spatial/temporal links. Transitive active verbs (*discuss, enter, reach*) do NOT take prepositions.
Use **Between** for 2 entities; use **Among** for more than 2 entities.
Sentences starting with *No sooner / Hardly / Scarcely* require inverted word order (**Verb before Subject**).
Always enforce fixed pairs: **No sooner...than**, **Hardly...when**, **Scarcely...when**, **Not only...but also**.
Interjections express sudden emotions (*Hurrah!, Alas!, Oh!*) and are followed by an exclamation mark.

upscNotes.content: UPSSSC PET Strategy: In Spotting Error questions, first identify the main verb and trace back to its true grammatical subject to quickly catch Subject-Verb Agreement errors.

Exam Trap: Examiners frequently place long prepositional phrases between the subject and verb (e.g., 'The quality of these mangoes ARE not good'). Don't fall for the plural noun near the verb; the subject is 'quality' (singular), so use 'IS'.
Fast Elimination Trick: If an option uses 'more senior than' or 'senior than', eliminate it instantly. The only correct form is 'senior to'.
Exam Trap: Watch out for 'No sooner...WHEN' or 'No sooner...THEN'. UPSSSC PET intentionally confuses candidates with incorrect conjunction pairings. Always look for 'THAN'.
Bilingual Advantage: Translate 'Beside' as 'पास में' (location) and 'Besides' as 'के अलावा' (addition) to instantly solve prepositions questions without confusion.

keyTakeaways: Uncountable nouns (advice, furniture, information, scenery) are ALWAYS singular and take no 'a/an' or '-s/-es'.
Subject-Verb Agreement: 'Neither...nor' matches the NEAREST subject; 'Along with / As well as' matches the FIRST subject.
Latin comparatives (senior, junior, superior, inferior) and 'preferable' take 'TO', never 'than'.
Correlative Pair Golden Formula: No sooner...THAN | Hardly/Scarcely...WHEN.
Active transitive verbs (discuss, describe, reach, order, resemble) take NO prepositions directly after them.
'Between' is strictly for 2 entities; 'Among' is for 3 or more entities.
'Beside' indicates physical proximity (next to); 'Besides' indicates addition (in addition to).

practice.question: Spot the error in the given sentence: 'The sceneries of Kashmir (A) / are so enchanting (B) / that thousands of tourists visit it every year. (C) / No error (D)'
options: that thousands of tourists visit it every year.
practice.explanation: 'Scenery' is an uncountable noun and does not have a plural form like 'sceneries'. The correct phrase should be 'The scenery of Kashmir'. Consequently, the verb should also be singular ('is so enchanting').

practice.question: Fill in the blank with the appropriate preposition: 'He is senior _____ me in service, but he treats me like a friend.'
practice.explanation: Comparative adjectives ending in '-ior' (such as senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior) take the preposition 'to' instead of 'than'.

practice.question: Improve the underlined part of the sentence: 'She sang *very sweet* at the concert last night.'
practice.explanation: The word modifies the verb 'sang', so an adverb of manner ('sweetly') is required instead of the adjective ('sweet'). Hence, 'very sweetly' is the correct choice.

practice.question: Spot the error in the given sentence: 'Each of the students (A) / must bring (B) / their own notebook to the class. (C) / No error (D)'
options: their own notebook to the class.
practice.explanation: 'Each' is an indefinite distributive pronoun that takes a singular verb and singular possessive pronoun. Therefore, 'their' should be replaced with 'his' or 'his/her'.

practice.question: Fill in the blank with the correct conjunction: 'Scarcely had the teacher entered the classroom _____ the students stood up to greet him.'
practice.explanation: 'Scarcely' and 'Hardly' are always paired with the conjunction 'when' (or 'before'), whereas 'No sooner' is paired with 'than'.

practice.question: Select the correct indirect form of the sentence: He said, 'I am buying a new car today.'
options: He said that he was buying a new car today.
He said that he was buying a new car that day.
He said that I was buying a new car that day.
He said that he is buying a new car that day.
practice.explanation: In indirect speech, present continuous ('am buying') changes to past continuous ('was buying'), the pronoun 'I' changes to 'he' according to the speaker, and 'today' changes to 'that day'.

practice.question: Improve the underlined part of the sentence: 'She works *hardly* to support her family.'
practice.explanation: 'Hardly' is an adverb meaning 'scarcely/barely', which alters the intended meaning. 'Hard' functions as an adverb meaning 'with great effort'. Therefore, 'works hard' is the correct expression.

practice.question: Spot the error in the given sentence: 'Neither Rahul nor his friends (A) / has attended (B) / the meeting today. (C) / No error (D)'
practice.explanation: When two subjects are joined by 'Neither... nor', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it. Since 'his friends' is plural, the verb should be plural ('have attended').

practice.question: Fill in the blank with the correct preposition: 'The magistrate acquitted him _____ all the charges leveled against him.'
practice.explanation: The verb 'acquitted' takes the fixed preposition 'of' when referring to criminal charges or accusations (e.g., acquitted of a crime).

practice.question: Improve the underlined part of the sentence: 'This task is *more easier* than the previous one.'
practice.explanation: Using 'more' alongside an adjective that already has '-er' creates a double comparative, which is grammatically incorrect. 'Easier' alone is sufficient.

practice.question: Select the correct indirect speech form: Rohan said to me, 'Can you lend me your book?'
options: Rohan asked me if I could lend him my book.
Rohan asked me that if I can lend him my book.
Rohan asked me if can I lend him my book.
Rohan requested me if I could lend him his book.
practice.explanation: In interrogative sentences starting with modal verbs: 'said to' changes to 'asked', conjunction 'if/whether' is used (not 'that if'), modal 'can' becomes 'could', word order becomes assertive (subject before verb), and pronouns shift ('you' -> 'I', 'me' -> 'him', 'your' -> 'my').

practice.question: Spot the error in the given sentence: 'This is the same dog (A) / who bit my brother (B) / yesterday evening. (C) / No error (D)'
practice.explanation: When the antecedent is preceded by 'the same', the relative pronoun 'that' is used instead of 'who' or 'which'.

practice.question: Fill in the blank with the correct verb form: 'My mother prevents me from _____ out in the rain.'
practice.explanation: The verb phrase 'prevent from' is followed by a gerund (verb + -ing form). Thus, 'going' is grammatically correct.

practice.question: Improve the underlined part of the sentence: 'He gave me two *five-hundreds rupees* notes yesterday.'
practice.explanation: When a compound numerical noun functions as a modifying adjective before a head noun ('notes'), it must remain in singular form ('five-hundred rupee').

practice.question: Select the correct indirect speech form: The master said to the servant, 'Bring me a glass of water.'
options: The master ordered the servant to bring him a glass of water.
The master said to the servant that bring him a glass of water.
The master ordered the servant that he should bring a glass of water.
The master requested the servant to bring me a glass of water.
practice.explanation: For imperative commands: reporting verb 'said to' changes to 'ordered', the infinitive 'to' connects the reported clause, and the pronoun 'me' shifts to 'him' according to the subject 'the master'.

pyqs.question: Which of the following words is an Adverb?
pyqs.explanation: 'Quickly' is an adverb because it modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb (formed by adding '-ly' to 'quick'). 'Careful' and 'Honest' are adjectives, while 'Beauty' is a noun.

pyqs.question: Identify the Abstract Noun in the sentence: 'His courage saved the day.'
pyqs.explanation: 'Courage' is an abstract noun as it represents an intangible quality that cannot be physically touched or seen. 'His' is a possessive pronoun/determiner, 'saved' is a verb, and 'day' is a common noun.

pyqs.question: Choose the correct part of speech for the underlined word: 'He came **after** I had left.'
pyqs.explanation: 'After' acts as a Conjunction here because it joins two clauses ('He came' and 'I had left'). When 'after' is followed by a full clause with a subject and verb, it functions as a subordinating conjunction.

pyqs.question: Identify the Adjective in the following sentence: 'The clever fox jumped over the fence.'
pyqs.explanation: 'Clever' is an adjective modifying the noun 'fox' by describing its trait/quality. 'Fox' and 'fence' are nouns, and 'jumped' is a verb.

pyqs.question: Which part of speech is the word 'Fast' in the sentence: 'He runs fast'?
pyqs.explanation: 'Fast' is an Adverb in this context because it modifies the action verb 'runs' by explaining how he runs. If it were describing a noun (e.g., 'a fast runner'), it would be an adjective.

pyqs.question: Identify the Pronoun in the given sentence: 'Neither of the two students was present.'
pyqs.explanation: 'Neither' functions as a Distributive Pronoun referring to 'not one nor the other of two persons'. 'Students' is a noun, 'present' acts as an adjective, and 'two' is a numeral adjective.

pyqs.question: Choose the appropriate Preposition to complete the sentence: 'She has been living in Delhi _____ 2015.'
pyqs.explanation: 'Since' is used as a preposition of time to denote a specific starting point in the past (2015) in Perfect / Perfect Continuous tenses. 'For' is used for a duration/period of time.

pyqs.question: What part of speech is the underlined word? '**Alas!** We lost the match.'
pyqs.explanation: 'Alas!' is an Interjection used to express a sudden outburst of emotion or sorrow, typically followed by an exclamation mark.

pyqs.question: Choose the correct Collective Noun to complete the sentence: 'A _____ of wolves attacked the livestock.'
pyqs.explanation: The standard collective noun for a group of wolves or hounds is 'Pack'. 'Herd' is used for cattle, 'Flock' for sheep or birds, and 'Swarm' for insects.

pyqs.question: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word: 'The water was **very** cold.'
pyqs.explanation: 'Very' is an Adverb of Degree modifying the adjective 'cold'. An adverb can modify a verb, an adjective, or another adverb.

test.question: Identify the part of speech of the word in uppercase: 'HONESTY is the best policy.'
test.explanation: 'Honesty' is an Abstract Noun because it names a quality that cannot be physically touched or seen.

test.question: Identify the part of speech of the word in uppercase: 'EACH of the boys received a gift.'
test.explanation: 'Each' is used here as a Distributive Pronoun because it refers to individuals in a group separately without directly modifying a noun.

test.question: Identify the part of speech of the word in uppercase: 'She wears a BEAUTIFUL dress.'
test.explanation: 'Beautiful' describes the noun 'dress', so it is an Adjective.

test.question: Identify the part of speech of the word in uppercase: 'The baby CRIED loudly.'
test.explanation: 'Cried' denotes the action performed by the subject ('the baby'), making it a Verb.

test.question: In the sentence 'He runs FAST', what part of speech is the word 'FAST'?
test.explanation: 'Fast' modifies the verb 'runs' (describing how he runs), making it an Adverb in this context.

test.question: Identify the part of speech of the word in uppercase: 'The book is ON the table.'
test.explanation: 'On' shows the spatial relationship between the noun 'book' and 'table', making it a Preposition.

test.question: Identify the part of speech of the word in uppercase: 'She wanted to go, BUT it was raining.'
test.explanation: 'But' connects two independent clauses ('She wanted to go' and 'it was raining'), making it a Coordinating Conjunction.

test.question: Identify the part of speech of the word in uppercase: 'HURRAH! We won the match.'
test.explanation: 'Hurrah!' is an Interjection used to express a sudden feeling of joy or triumph.

test.question: In the sentence 'This is a FAST train', what part of speech is the word 'FAST'?
test.explanation: 'Fast' modifies the noun 'train' (describing the type of train), making it an Adjective in this context.

test.question: Identify the part of speech of the word in uppercase: 'A HERD of cattle was grazing in the field.'
test.explanation: 'Herd' refers to a collection or group of animals taken as a whole, making it a Collective Noun.
